title: Timing Attacks — Early Exit vs Constant Time

questions.question: What does an “early-exit” byte comparison do on a mismatch?
options: Stops immediately when it finds the first differing byte
Continues comparing all bytes and accumulates differences
Always pads both inputs to a fixed length first
Encrypts both inputs before comparing them
questions.explanation: Early-exit comparisons return as soon as they see a mismatch.

questions.question: What is the attacker’s advantage in a timing attack?
options: They can learn information correlated with secrets by measuring runtime
They can directly read memory from the target process
They can always recover the private key in one request
They can bypass authentication without any guesses
questions.explanation: Timing provides a side channel: it correlates with secret-dependent control flow.

questions.question: Why can an early-exit token comparison leak the token one byte at a time?
options: Guesses with a longer correct prefix run longer, so timing reveals prefix length
Tokens are always ASCII, making them easier to brute force
Network packets contain the token twice
TLS encryption is deterministic
questions.explanation: The runtime correlates with how many bytes matched before the first mismatch.

questions.question: Which property best defines a constant-time comparison routine?
options: Its control flow and work do not depend on secret data values
It has a low average runtime
It uses constant memory
It runs in exactly one CPU cycle
questions.explanation: Constant-time means no secret-dependent branches/early exits (at a practical level).

questions.question: In Python, which standard library function is designed for constant-time equality checks of authentication data?
options: hmac.compare_digest
hashlib.sha256
base64.b64encode
secrets.token_hex
questions.explanation: `hmac.compare_digest` is intended to mitigate timing leaks in comparisons.

questions.question: Why is adding random delay on failures not a reliable fix for timing attacks?
options: Attackers can average out noise over many requests and recover the signal statistically
It turns the comparison into constant-time automatically
It prevents attackers from making requests at all
It makes tokens unguessable
questions.explanation: Noise reduces signal quality but often doesn’t remove it; repeated sampling can recover it.

questions.question: Which ordering is safer when verifying attacker-controlled encrypted/authenticated data?
options: Verify integrity/authenticity first, then parse/decrypt
Parse/decrypt first, then verify authenticity only if parsing succeeded
Return detailed errors for each failure stage
Retry parsing with multiple fallback formats
questions.explanation: Authenticity checks should happen before expensive or detail-leaking parsing/decryption.

questions.question: What is an “oracle” in the context of timing attacks?
options: Any interface that leaks a measurable signal correlated with a secret
A database that stores secrets safely
A randomness source used for nonces
A public key used for encryption
questions.explanation: An oracle can be timing, error codes, response lengths—anything observable per query.
